title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 141 (Eligibility and disqualifications of auditors)

content.overview: Section 141 lets a chartered accountant, or a firm whose majority of partners practising in India are chartered accountants, be appointed auditor. A body corporate, an officer or employee, a person indebted to the company beyond the prescribed amount, and a person holding the securities the section bars, are disqualified.
content.glance: A chartered accountant, or a firm whose majority of partners are chartered accountants, may be appointed auditor, subject to the disqualifications in the section.
content.study:
## Statutory rule
Section 141(1) says a person is eligible for appointment as auditor only if he is a chartered accountant. A firm whose majority of partners practising in India are qualified for appointment may be appointed by its firm name.

Section 141(3) disqualifies a body corporate other than a limited liability partnership, an officer or employee of the company, a partner or employee of an officer or employee, a person indebted to the company or its related companies for an amount exceeding the prescribed amount, a person who has given a guarantee in connection with the indebtedness of a third person to the company for such amount, a person holding any security of or interest in the company or its related companies as the section describes, and a person in full-time employment elsewhere.

Section 141(4) makes an appointment in contravention void, and a disqualification after appointment a vacation of office.

## Answer structure
Eligibility is the chartered-accountant qualification. Then check the subsection (3) bars. Not a verified closure.

sections.heading: Rule
sections.body: A chartered accountant, or a firm whose majority of partners are chartered accountants, may be appointed auditor, subject to the disqualifications in the section.

sections.heading: Explanation
sections.body: Disqualifications include a body corporate other than an LLP, an officer or employee, a person or relative or partner with a prescribed business relationship or security interest, a person indebted beyond the limit, and a person convicted of fraud for the stated period. The auditor must be independent in the sense the section defines. Holding appointment in more than the prescribed number of companies is a bar.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.
